title: The court letter's next step
hook: Would a clearer summons and a reminder change missed appearances?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Distinguish ability to act on a notice from fear of the underlying penalty.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Distinguish ability to act on a notice from fear of the underlying penalty.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy notice requires three steps of five minutes each to respond. What response time does that procedure require? Toy inputs A=[3, 5, 50]; B=[1, 5, 50].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[15, 3, 50], [5, 1, 50]]. Labels: Minutes to act, Steps, Penalty €.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The comparison simplifies the procedure while keeping the stated penalty fixed. Clear next actions and penalty severity are different levers. A lower procedural burden does not by itself establish a measured change in attendance.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Action steps=1, Minutes/step=5, Penalty €=50. What is Minutes to act? Answer: 5.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Action steps=1, Minutes/step=5, Penalty €=50. What is Minutes to act?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 5. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.section: 19. Public policy nudges: tax, energy, voting
sourceProvenance.text: Redesigned court summonses and text reminders cut missed court dates in New York by 13–21% (Fishbane, Ouss & Shah, 2020).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Distinguish ability to act on a notice from fear of the underlying penalty.
